title: Course 3 / Data Engineering 2026 — Detailed Study Guide

parts.title: 1. Your route and a realistic time budget

lines.text: Data Engineering 2026 has 10 modules and 140 controlled units.

The module planning ranges stored in this edition total about 67-140 focused study days. These are planning budgets, not promises or deadlines. Gates, repairs, setup problems and repeated practice can add time.
A study day means focused learning and practical work. Do not estimate the course by PDF page count: a short technical page can require more practice than a long explanation.
Judge completion by evidence: you can perform the main action, validate the result and explain why it is correct. Watching or rereading alone is study in progress, not mastery.

rows: C3-07 · Cloud / Microsoft Fabric Data Engineering

lines.text: Use six focused study days and one recovery day if that rhythm fits you. More hours are optional; do not stack new lessons while today’s practical attempt is unfinished.
Keep the downloaded course ZIP unchanged as a recovery copy. Extract it and work from the ordinary extracted folder; do not edit files while browsing inside the ZIP.

In the Mentor, open How to study first, then choose C3-00 and start C3-00-L01 · Role shift: analyst scripts -> engineering systems. The first teaching book is assets/C3-00/C3_010_ENGINEERING_FOUNDATIONS_BEGINNER_FIRST_LESSON_BOOK_RC1.pdf. The mapped practice route is assets/C3-00/C3_011_ENGINEERING_FOUNDATIONS_PRACTICE_PACK_RC1.pdf.

Use a laptop/PC for Linux/WSL2, Git, Python, ingestion, dbt/SQL, Airflow, lakehouse/Parquet, Spark, Kafka/streaming, Fabric/cloud and DataOps controls. A phone is useful beside the laptop for PDFs, mapped videos and revision, but it does not replace practical work that requires the native tool.
Open only the files the current lesson asks for. Later software and cloud tools should be opened or installed when their module requires them; do not create extra setup work at the beginning.
The Mentor is a front door and tracker, not a substitute for saved artifacts. Its evidence box stores text; keep the real workbook/query/notebook/script/report/project files on your computer.

parts.title: 3. A six-hour day you can follow

lines.text: Use this as a routine, not an examination timetable. If a video is short, put the spare time into practice. If setup fails, that session becomes setup repair; do not mark the lesson complete just because the clock ended.

rows: Close notes. Explain one idea and repeat one small action from memory.
Open one lesson, read purpose/prerequisites and locate named inputs.
Use only the assigned range/source; pause, predict and connect it to the written lesson.
Perform the guided steps yourself in the real tool and inspect the result.
Close the answer/example and make the independent or changed attempt.
Validate. Open protected review only after saving an attempt; repair the cause and retry.
Save evidence, explain the result aloud and write the exact next lesson/step.

lines.text: Total: 360 focused minutes. Breaks, meals, downloads running unattended and scrolling are outside the six hours. The optional Mentor stopwatch never gates a lesson; there is no compulsory 25-minute rule.

parts.title: 4. How one lesson becomes a skill

lines.text: Step 1 — Locate the task
Find the guided example, independent/changed task and validation rule. If you cannot say what you are meant to produce, do not start clicking or typing yet.
Step 2 — Read a small amount
Read the purpose, vocabulary and prerequisites. State the aim in one plain sentence before opening the tool.
Step 3 — Watch with a question
Use the assigned video/source only for the stated scope. Know what you are looking for; pause after meaningful steps and predict what should happen next.
Step 4 — Reproduce the worked example

Perform the example yourself. In this course that may produce shell commands, Git history, Python packages, ingestion jobs, dbt/SQL transformations, Airflow workflows, lakehouse/Spark/streaming work, Fabric/cloud exercises and production runbooks. Inspect intermediate results instead of copying a finished answer blindly.
Step 5 — Make an independent attempt
Save the guided example, close the protected answer, and solve the printed task or changed input yourself. An error is part of the attempt; preserve it.
Step 6 — Validate
Use the lesson’s controls: counts, totals, grain, keys, refresh state, model relationships, expected columns, files, tests or other checks that actually matter.
Step 7 — Review and retry

After saving the first attempt, open only the matching protected review. Identify the first reasoning difference, close it, repair the weakness, then complete the changed/fresh retry with the review closed.
Step 8 — Finish only when you have evidence
You can reproduce the main action, check the result and explain why it works. The Mentor’s Complete button records your judgement; it is not automatic grading.

parts.title: 5. A real example from your opening module

lines.text: C3-00-L02 is not a Linux vocabulary lesson only. You should be able to identify the current path, navigate to the correct project folder, inspect expected files and avoid running a command in the wrong directory.

C3-00-L04 turns Git into evidence. A saved file is useful; a commit history that shows the change, message and recoverable state is stronger engineering proof. Follow the course workflow rather than treating GitHub as file storage.

C3-00-L12 introduces a standard used throughout Course 3: rerunning the documented process should not silently duplicate or corrupt the result. Save the state before/after the rerun and explain what makes the operation reproducible.

parts.title: 7. Files, attempts and notes without extra busywork

lines.text: Use one stable working area such as Documents/C3_Data_Engineering. Keep the original course ZIP separately. Inside the working area, use module ID and lesson ID so evidence is easy to find; for example, Documents/C3_Data_Engineering/C3-00/C3-00-L01.

If the lesson supplies a filename, preserve it where practical. If it asks you to create a query, script, workbook, report, model, diagram or explanation, save the thing you made plus the result that proves it worked.
Artifact means the thing you created. Evidence means the saved result that supports your claim. Neither requires a decorative report unless the lesson asks for one.

Keep the teaching book as your main notes. Maintain only a small mistake log: lesson ID, what failed, why it failed and what fixed it. Recopying the textbook into a second notebook does not prove skill.

At the end of the week, copy your work to a second location you control. Export the Mentor progress backup before clearing browser data or moving devices. Phone and PC progress do not synchronize automatically.
After the last lesson of a module, use its quick-revision surface with the book closed first. Then attempt the module practical/mastery test and save the result before opening the protected review.

Gate A is the normal fresh Gate. Preserve the full attempt before Review A. Repair the named weak skill, then attempt the genuinely different Gate B only when the course state assigns it. Later remediation variants never erase the need to keep the original attempt.

Protected/sealed means a study-order rule; the file is not magically grading you. Do not move ahead after copying a review. Use the course’s own success criteria and return to the named weak lesson when needed.

parts.title: 9. What to do when you are stuck

lines.text: First separate ‘I do not understand the idea’ from ‘the tool reports an error’. For an idea, ask for a tiny example and define the unfamiliar word. For an error, preserve the exact message, command/action and current file/folder/model context.

Try a short diagnosis: reread the immediately preceding step; check filename/path/table/model/tool; compare the smallest input with the worked example; change one suspected cause and rerun. Do not make five unrelated changes at once.

Preserve the full error, command, current folder, tool/version and smallest input that reproduces it. For Docker/Airflow/Spark/Kafka/Fabric problems, distinguish setup failure from lesson-logic failure. Never paste secrets; share only sanitized configuration and the exact visible error.

When asking ChatGPT or another helper, include the course/lesson ID and relevant excerpt because another chat may not have your package. Ask for one hint first, run it yourself, then show the result. Do not reveal the protected answer before your own attempt.
Never paste passwords, API keys, private account tokens or personal datasets. Share sanitized column names, harmless sample rows and the smallest code/error needed to reproduce the problem.

parts.title: 10. What the video/source labels really mean

lines.text: A source beside a lesson is a visual/official aid assigned to that lesson. It does not mean the recording teaches every sentence in the book. The written lesson defines your exact practical task, files and validation rules.

A bounded timestamp means watch that range and stop manually. A reused visual means you already saw that source; rewatch only what you need. If a source has no verified bounded range, use its published chapters/topic context instead of automatically watching a multi-hour recording again.
Videos may use a different dataset, UI version or business story. Do not rewrite the course task to match the video. Follow the course’s supplied files and version notes.

No generated video lesson is required. If a mapped source disappears, keep learning from the complete written explanation and report the lesson ID/title/link for repair; do not invent a replacement URL.

C3_09 is the production capstone and engineering transition. Build it as an operational system, not a collection of screenshots: source contract, ingestion, transformation, orchestration, storage/processing, quality/observability, recovery evidence, runbook and architecture defense. State honestly which engines you ran natively and which you only simulated.

For any project or capstone, establish an expected result with the supplied fixture/input first, then test changed input and recovery as the project asks. Keep failed-run evidence when it explains a repair; reproducibility is not the same as hiding failures.
Your daily finish line is simple: I made something, checked it and can explain it. If you only watched or read today, record study in progress and make the practical attempt your next step.
